parsed_answer.content: A spurious wakeup is a phenomenon in multithreaded programming where a thread waiting on a synchronization primitive, such as a Java Object monitor (via wait()), is awakened from its waiting state even though no other thread has explicitly called notify() or notifyAll(). This behavior is not a bug in the JVM, but rather a design concession to the underlying operating system's thread scheduling primitives (like POSIX threads). On many platforms, ensuring that a thread is only woken up by a signal is computationally expensive; allowing spurious wakeups permits the OS kernel to be more efficient. Consequently, a thread that was blocked on a condition might suddenly find itself in a runnable state without the condition it was waiting for actually being met. Failure to account for this leads to race conditions where a thread proceeds with invalid state assumptions, potentially corrupting shared resources or violating business invariants.

items: The wait() method must always be enclosed in a 'while' loop rather than an 'if' statement. The loop ensures that upon waking, the thread re-evaluates the predicate condition.
When a thread wakes up, it must re-acquire the object's monitor lock before it can proceed, which naturally serializes access and allows the thread to check the state again.
The condition being checked must be a shared variable protected by the same monitor lock used for the wait() call, ensuring visibility across threads via the happens-before relationship.
Spurious wakeups are non-deterministic; they can occur at any time, making them notoriously difficult to reproduce in local development environments without stress testing.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Engineer Insight: Never assume that waking up from a wait() implies your condition is true. If you use an 'if' statement instead of a 'while' loop, you are essentially creating a 'time-of-check to time-of-use' (TOCTOU) vulnerability. In high-concurrency systems, this is a common source of intermittent 'IndexOutOfBoundsException' or 'NullPointerException' errors that only appear under heavy load when the OS scheduler is forced to context-switch frequently.

title: Explain Spurious Wakeups in threading and how to write loop checks to avoid them.
